newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Bahrain's cheap market attracts Gulf investors.
newsitem.headline: Bahrain's cheap market attracts Gulf investors.

text.p: Gulf Arab investors, increasingly confident, are fuelling a booming market by buying heavily into Bahraini shares as analysts say there are bargains there for the taking.
Dealers and bankers say the Bahrain stock exchange has been rising since the start of the year and further gains of around 10 percent are likely by year-end.

"Sentiment is positive in the market on expectation that banks' end-year results will be good. I expect the index to grow to between 1,900-2,000 points by the end of the year," a market analyst told Reuters on Tuesday.

The index rose to 1,803.54 points on Sunday, the highest level this year. This is 16.6 percent higher than its 1,546.03 point close on January 2. During 1996 the index rose by over 16 percent from 1,325.04 points at end-1995.
"I expect the index to continue its upward trend until the end of the year," a dealer said.
"The Bahraini market is the cheapest in the Gulf. The emergence of new Gulf Arab investors has helped increase demand despite the usually quiet summer trade," another trader said.
"Gulf Arab investors are in the Bahraini market. They have brought in good liquidity. Some Gulf investors have switched their bank deposits to stocks," one dealer said.
Cash-rich investors from other Gulf Arab states -- Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait -- can own up to 49 percent in Bahraini listed firms.
Activity has also picked up this year. Over 232 million shares were traded in the first half, 126 percent up on first half 1996. For full 1996, some 299 million shares were dealt.
Dealers said trade this year has focused on banks and investment firms, whose market capitalisation rose to 1.13 billion dinars ($3 billion) at end-June 1997 from one billion a year earlier.
There are 40 firms listed on the exchange with a market capitalisation of more than 1.7 billion dinars.
Bankers said Bahrain was undervalued, with a price-earnings ratio of 11.5 compared with around 15 in nearby Oman and around 20 in Kuwait.

A banker said Gulf investors had been cautious in investing in regional shares since the 1991 Gulf War ending Iraq's occupation of Kuwait. "They now find good profitability in the market and are investing heavily in Bahrain stocks."

Bahrain is the Gulf's main financial and banking hub. There were now around 40 offshore banking units operating in Bahrain and their assets climbed to $68.80 billion at end-March 1997 from $62.50 billion a year earlier.

Taib Bank said commercial banks were under-performing this year. All listed commercial banks, with the exception of Bank of Bahrain and Kuwait (BBK), announced lower operating profit before provisions for the first half of 1997.
BBK, the second largest commercial bank in the island, lifted first half net profit over 14 percent.
Shares of Bahrain Middle East Bank (BMB) have dominated trading in the past month. The bank's share climbed to 169 fils on Monday from 140 fils each a month earlier.
"This degree of hyper-activity in BMB is based on expectations that the bank's earnings are already more than double of the earnings for whole of 1996," Taib Bank said.

"The same logic is fuelling the rise in the price for United Gulf Bank shares which have closed at 165 fils each last week, up 11 percent from the closing price of 148 fils in the prior week," it added.
Bahrain's bourse is open to nationals in Gulf Arab states. Some firms are also open to foreign investors.
-- Bahrain newsroom 973-524424.
